## Oct 4 Results: The Numbers Tell a Split Story

Let's talk data. Yesterday we went 1-1, landing at exactly 50.0% accuracy. Not the percentage we're chasing, but the sample size is small and variance happens. Let me break down what the model saw versus what actually happened on the field.

## The Miss Analysis

The Dodgers pick at 63% confidence didn't hit. That's baseball. Even 63% probability means the Braves had a 37% chance—roughly 1 in 3 games. When you're dealing with probabilities, you have to accept that high-confidence picks will sometimes fall on the wrong side of variance.

## Oct 5 Preview: Cleveland Shows Strong Value

Now let's pivot to tomorrow's slate. The data is pointing to one game in particular: White Sox at Guardians. The model is projecting a 61% win probability for Cleveland, and when you look at the pitching matchup, the numbers support it.

## Why Cleveland at 61%?

The pitching differential is significant here. Gavin Williams at home gives Cleveland an edge that the model quantifies at 61%. That's above our 60% threshold for high-confidence plays. Anthony Kay on the road for the White Sox doesn't present the same statistical profile.

Look at it this way: 61% isn't a guarantee, but it represents value. Over a large sample size, backing 61% probabilities will produce positive returns. That's what we're tracking here—long-term edge, not single-game certainty.

## The Bottom Line

Oct 4 went 50-50. That's variance. Oct 5 presents a 61% edge with Cleveland. The model doesn't care about yesterday—it only processes current data. And right now, the data says Guardians.

We track every pick, every probability, every result. That's how you find edge over time. Check back tomorrow for the Oct 5 results breakdown.
